topics.name: Classification and Structure of Amines
topics.summary: Amines are derivatives of ammonia (NH3) formed by replacing one, two, or three hydrogen atoms with alkyl/aryl groups, giving primary (1°, RNH2), secondary (2°, R2NH), and tertiary (3°, R3N) amines respectively -- this classification is based on the number of carbon groups attached to nitrogen, NOT the type of carbon (unlike alcohols/halides, where 1°/2°/3° refers to the carbon itself). Amines can be aliphatic (only alkyl groups) or aromatic (at least one aryl group directly attached to N, e.g., aniline C6H5NH2). Nitrogen in amines is sp3 hybridized and pyramidal, like ammonia, with a lone pair occupying the fourth position; this lone pair is responsible for both basicity and nucleophilicity. Because the nitrogen is pyramidal, an amine with three different groups is technically chiral, but rapid pyramidal inversion (through a planar sp2 transition state) interconverts the two configurations so fast that separate enantiomers cannot be isolated. In aromatic amines such as aniline, the nitrogen lone pair partially delocalizes into the benzene ring by resonance, flattening the geometry somewhat and reducing the lone pair's availability compared with an aliphatic amine.
key_formulas: 1° amine: R-NH2 (one C-N bond)
2° amine: R2NH (two C-N bonds)
3° amine: R3N (three C-N bonds)
Quaternary ammonium salt: R4N+X− (four C-N bonds, no lone pair on N)
topics.worked_example: Classify CH3-NH-CH3: nitrogen bears two methyl groups and one H, i.e., two C-N bonds → secondary (2°) amine, specifically dimethylamine.
common_mistakes: Classifying amines by the carbon they're attached to (as with alcohols) instead of by the number of alkyl/aryl groups on nitrogen -- (CH3)3C-NH2 is a primary amine even though it is attached to a tertiary carbon.
Assuming amines with three different N-substituents are isolable as separate enantiomers, ignoring rapid pyramidal inversion at nitrogen.
Treating aniline's nitrogen as identical in hybridization/geometry to an aliphatic amine's nitrogen, missing the resonance-induced partial flattening.

topics.name: Nomenclature of Amines
topics.summary: Amine nomenclature uses both common and IUPAC systems. Common names attach 'amine' to the alkyl group name for simple 1° amines (methylamine); symmetrical 2°/3° amines use di-/tri- prefixes (dimethylamine, trimethylamine); unsymmetrical 2°/3° amines list the alkyl groups alphabetically before 'amine' (ethylmethylamine). IUPAC names primary amines as alkanamines, replacing the terminal '-e' of the parent alkane with '-amine' (ethanamine for CH3CH2NH2). For unsymmetrical secondary/tertiary amines, the LARGEST group is chosen as the parent alkanamine, and the remaining group(s) on nitrogen are cited as N-substituents with an italic capital N-locant (N-methylethanamine for CH3-NH-C2H5). When the amino group is not the senior functional group of the molecule, -NH2 is cited as the substituent prefix 'amino-'. Aniline is a retained IUPAC name for aminobenzene (benzenamine/phenylamine are also acceptable); its N-substituted derivatives, such as N,N-dimethylaniline, place the italic N-locants before the substituent names to show they sit on the ring nitrogen, not on the ring carbons.
key_formulas: IUPAC 1° amine: alkane + amine (drop 'e'): CH3CH2NH2 = ethanamine
N-locant for a substituent on N: CH3-NH-C2H5 = N-methylethanamine
Aromatic 1° amine: C6H5NH2 = aniline (retained name)
-NH2 as a substituent prefix (not the senior group): amino-
topics.worked_example: Name CH3-CH2-NH-CH3 by IUPAC: the larger group on nitrogen (ethyl, 2 carbons) is chosen as the parent 'ethanamine'; the smaller group (methyl) attached to nitrogen is cited with an italic N-locant → N-methylethanamine.
common_mistakes: Naming unsymmetrical secondary/tertiary amines without first picking the LARGEST group as the parent chain, so the N-locant ends up on the wrong substituent.
Forgetting that -NH2 must be cited as 'amino-' (not 'amine-') when it is not the senior functional group of a more complex molecule.
Confusing an N-substituted aniline (substituent on nitrogen, e.g., N-methylaniline) with a ring-substituted toluidine (substituent on the ring carbon, e.g., o-toluidine).

topics.name: Preparation of Amines
topics.summary: Several independent routes give amines. (1) Ammonolysis of alkyl/benzyl halides: RX + excess NH3 (sealed tube, heat) gives a 1° amine, but that amine is itself nucleophilic and reacts further with more RX to give 2°, 3°, and quaternary ammonium salt as a mixture -- this route is therefore poor for a single pure product, and it cannot be used on aryl halides at all (which resist nucleophilic substitution under ordinary conditions). (2) Reduction of nitro compounds: ArNO2, with H2/catalyst or Fe/HCl or Sn/HCl, gives ArNH2 -- the industrial route to aniline. (3) Reduction of nitriles: RCN, with H2/Ni or LiAlH4, gives RCH2NH2, a primary amine with one carbon MORE than the alkyl halide originally used to make the nitrile (because the cyanide carbon itself becomes part of the product). (4) Reduction of amides: RCONH2 with LiAlH4 gives RCH2NH2. (5) Reductive amination: an aldehyde or ketone plus NH3 (or an amine) with H2/Ni gives the corresponding amine, the carbon skeleton and any branching of the carbonyl compound being carried over into the amine product.
key_formulas: RX + excess NH3 → RNH2 (+ 2°, 3°, and quaternary salt as side products)
ArNO2 + 6[H] (Fe/HCl, Sn/HCl, or H2/Ni) → ArNH2 + 2H2O
RCN + 4[H] (H2/Ni or LiAlH4) → RCH2NH2
RCONH2 + 4[H] (LiAlH4) → RCH2NH2 + H2O
topics.worked_example: Prepare propan-1-amine from ethyl bromide via a nitrile: CH3CH2Br + NaCN → CH3CH2CN (propanenitrile) --H2/Ni--> CH3CH2CH2NH2 (propan-1-amine); the amine has one carbon more than the original bromide because the CN carbon is retained in the product.
common_mistakes: Assuming ammonolysis of an alkyl halide gives one clean primary amine product, ignoring the polyalkylation problem that yields a mixture of 1°/2°/3° amines and quaternary salt.

Forgetting that going from a nitrile to a primary amine (via reduction) does not by itself add or remove a carbon -- the extra carbon relative to the ORIGINAL HALIDE was already added earlier, at the cyanide-substitution step.

Trying to prepare aniline by ammonolysis of chlorobenzene under ordinary conditions, instead of recognising that aryl halides resist nucleophilic substitution and that aniline is made industrially by nitro-group reduction.

topics.name: Gabriel Synthesis and Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation
topics.summary: Two named routes each avoid the over-alkylation problem of direct ammonolysis. Gabriel phthalimide synthesis: phthalimide is treated with ethanolic KOH to form potassium phthalimide (the imide N-H is acidic, flanked by two carbonyls); this nucleophile is alkylated with a primary alkyl halide (SN2) to give N-alkylphthalimide, which on hydrolysis (acidic, alkaline, or hydrazinolysis) releases a pure primary amine plus phthalic acid/hydrazide -- since only one alkylation occurs, no over-alkylation is possible. This method fails for aromatic primary amines because aryl halides do not undergo the required nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion. Hoffmann bromamide degradation: a primary amide is treated with Br2 and excess NaOH; this converts RCONH2 into RNH2 with LOSS of the carbonyl carbon (lost as carbonate/CO2), proceeding through an N-bromoamide and then a nitrene/isocyanate (R-N=C=O) intermediate formed by migration of R from carbon to nitrogen -- a migration that proceeds with retention of configuration at the migrating group, making the reaction stereochemically informative.
key_formulas: Phthalimide + KOH → potassium phthalimide (nucleophilic N−)
Potassium phthalimide + RX → N-alkylphthalimide --hydrolysis--> RNH2 + phthalate salt
RCONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH → RNH2 + 2NaBr + Na2CO3 + 2H2O (one carbon lost)
topics.worked_example: Hoffmann degradation of CH3CH2CONH2 (propanamide, 3 carbons) with Br2/NaOH gives CH3CH2NH2 (ethanamine, 2 carbons) -- the carbonyl carbon is lost as part of the carbonate byproduct.
common_mistakes: Using Gabriel synthesis to try to prepare aniline or another aromatic primary amine, overlooking that aryl halides cannot undergo the required SN2 step with phthalimide anion.

Forgetting that Hoffmann bromamide degradation REDUCES the carbon count by one (amide → amine with one fewer carbon), and instead assuming the product retains the same number of carbons as the starting amide.
Treating phthalimide itself, rather than the alkyl halide used to alkylate it, as the source of the eventual amine's carbon skeleton in Gabriel synthesis.

topics.name: Physical Properties of Amines
topics.summary: Lower aliphatic amines (methyl-, dimethyl-, trimethylamine) are gases at room temperature with a characteristic ammonia-like/fishy smell; amines with more carbons are liquids, and higher members are solids. Primary and secondary amines carry N-H bonds and can hydrogen-bond with one another (N-H···N), giving higher boiling points than alkanes of similar molar mass but LOWER boiling points than alcohols of comparable mass, because nitrogen (less electronegative than oxygen) forms weaker hydrogen bonds. Among isomeric amines, primary generally boils higher than secondary, which boils higher than tertiary, because 1° amines offer two N-H hydrogen-bond donors per molecule, 2° amines offer one, and 3° amines (no N-H) cannot hydrogen-bond with each other at all -- though all three classes can still ACCEPT hydrogen bonds from water, so lower members of every class remain water-soluble. Water solubility falls off as the hydrophobic alkyl chain lengthens. Aniline and similar simple aromatic amines are colorless liquids that slowly darken (brown/pink) on exposure to air and light because of oxidation.
key_formulas: Boiling point among C-isomers: 1° > 2° > 3° amine (N-H donor count: 2 > 1 > 0)
bp trend for similar mass: alkane < amine < alcohol
Water solubility: high for lower amines of all classes (H-bond acceptor from water); falls with chain length
topics.worked_example: Among the C3H9N isomers 1-propanamine (1°, bp ≈48°C), N-methylethanamine (2°, bp ≈37°C), and trimethylamine (3°, bp ≈3°C), the primary amine boils highest because it has two N-H bonds enabling more extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding, while trimethylamine, with no N-H bond at all, boils lowest.
common_mistakes: Assuming amines boil higher than alcohols of similar molar mass, forgetting that nitrogen's lower electronegativity makes N-H···N bonds weaker than O-H···O bonds.
Ranking a tertiary amine as boiling highest among 1°/2°/3° isomers by assuming more alkyl substitution always raises boiling point, instead of counting available N-H hydrogen-bond donors.
Concluding that a tertiary amine, having no N-H, must be insoluble in water -- it can still accept hydrogen bonds from water as a proton acceptor, so lower tertiary amines stay water-soluble.

topics.name: Basicity of Amines
topics.summary: Amines are basic because the nitrogen lone pair can accept a proton. In the isolated gas phase (no solvent), basicity tracks electron density on nitrogen directly, so alkyl (+I, electron-donating) substitution raises basicity in the order 3° > 2° > 1° > NH3. In aqueous solution, however, the protonated ammonium cation must also be stabilised by hydrogen-bonding solvation with water, and a bulkier tertiary ammonium ion is more sterically hindered from that solvation; the NCERT-quoted order for methyl-substituted amines in water is therefore (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3 -- a balance of +I effect, steric hindrance, and cation solvation. Aromatic amines (aniline) are markedly WEAKER bases than ammonia or alkylamines because the nitrogen lone pair delocalizes into the benzene ring by resonance, leaving it less available to accept a proton. Electron-donating ring substituents (e.g., -CH3, -OCH3) increase aniline's basicity by adding electron density; electron-withdrawing groups (e.g., -NO2, -X) decrease it, with the effect strongest when the substituent sits ortho or para (direct resonance withdrawal) rather than meta.
key_formulas: Gas phase (no solvation): 3° > 2° > 1° > NH3 (pure +I effect)
Aqueous phase (methylamines): (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3
Basicity: alkylamine > NH3 > aniline (resonance delocalizes aniline's lone pair)
p-nitroaniline << aniline < p-toluidine (EWG lowers, EDG raises aromatic-amine basicity)
topics.worked_example: Rank NH3, CH3NH2, and C6H5NH2 by basicity: CH3NH2's methyl group donates electron density by +I, raising basicity above NH3; C6H5NH2 (aniline) is the weakest of the three because its lone pair is delocalized into the ring by resonance → CH3NH2 > NH3 > C6H5NH2.
common_mistakes: Applying the pure gas-phase +I order (3° > 2° > 1°) to an aqueous-solution basicity question, missing that steric hindrance to solvation drops (CH3)3N below (CH3)2NH and CH3NH2 in water.

Ranking aniline as more basic than ammonia by focusing only on the ring being 'electron-rich', rather than recognising that the NH2 lone pair itself is resonance-delocalized into the ring and thus less available to a proton.

Treating a meta-substituent's effect on aniline's basicity the same as an ortho/para substituent's effect, forgetting that resonance donation/withdrawal operates only through ortho and para positions.

topics.name: Acylation and Alkylation Reactions of Amines
topics.summary: Amines act as nucleophiles at nitrogen in two important reaction classes. Alkylation: reaction with alkyl halides proceeds through successive SN2 substitutions -- a 1° amine reacts further with more alkyl halide to give 2°, then 3°, then a quaternary ammonium salt, so this route (like direct ammonolysis) gives a mixture and is of limited use for cleanly making one amine. Acylation: 1° and 2° amines react with acid chlorides or acid anhydrides (often with a trace of pyridine to mop up the HCl formed) to give N-substituted amides -- acetanilide from aniline and acetic anhydride, for example. This reaction replaces an N-H with an acyl group and is used synthetically to 'protect' a primary aromatic amine's -NH2, moderating its powerful ring-activating effect before an electrophilic aromatic substitution is attempted; the acetyl group is later removed by acid or base hydrolysis to regenerate the free amine. A tertiary amine, having no N-H at all, cannot undergo this acylation (there is no hydrogen for the acyl group to replace), though it may still act as a base/catalyst in the mixture.
key_formulas: RNH2 + R'X → RR'NH + HX (continues on to R2R'N and eventually R3R'N+X−)
C6H5NH2 + (CH3CO)2O --pyridine--> C6H5NHCOCH3 (acetanilide) + CH3COOH
R2NH + CH3COCl → R2N-COCH3 + HCl
topics.worked_example: Aniline is converted to acetanilide with acetic anhydride (a trace of pyridine present); -NHCOCH3 is a much weaker ring activator than free -NH2, so acetanilide can be selectively mono-brominated at the para position before the acetyl group is hydrolyzed off to regenerate p-bromoaniline.
common_mistakes: Expecting a tertiary amine to undergo acylation with an acid chloride/anhydride the same way a 1°/2° amine does, overlooking that it has no N-H to be replaced.
Assuming alkylation of a primary amine with an alkyl halide stops cleanly at the secondary-amine stage, ignoring further reaction on to tertiary amine and quaternary ammonium salt.

Forgetting the actual purpose of acetylating aniline before electrophilic substitution (moderating the powerful activation of -NH2), and instead treating it as merely a way to change physical properties.

topics.name: Carbylamine Reaction and Reaction with Nitrous Acid
topics.summary: Two classic amine test reactions. Carbylamine (isocyanide) test: a primary amine (aliphatic OR aromatic), heated with chloroform and alcoholic KOH, forms an isocyanide (R-NC), recognised by its extremely foul, offensive smell; secondary and tertiary amines give NO such product, making this test diagnostic specifically for 1° amines. Reaction with nitrous acid (HNO2, generated in situ from NaNO2 + dilute HCl/H2SO4 at 0-5°C): a 1° ALIPHATIC amine forms a highly unstable diazonium salt that decomposes immediately, even at 0°C, with brisk evolution of N2 gas, giving a mixture of alcohol/alkene/alkyl-halide products -- the visible gas evolution is itself a positive test for a 1° aliphatic amine. A 1° AROMATIC amine (aniline) instead forms a diazonium salt that IS stable at 0-5°C -- the basis of diazotization. A 2° amine (aliphatic or aromatic) gives an N-nitrosamine (a yellow oily liquid, R2N-N=O). A 3° ALIPHATIC amine simply forms an unstable salt with HNO2 (no permanent product on the skeleton), while a 3° AROMATIC amine (e.g., N,N-dimethylaniline) undergoes ring electrophilic substitution at the para position to give a green, crystalline p-nitroso derivative.
key_formulas: RNH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH(alc.) → RNC (foul smell) + 3KCl + 3H2O (1° amines only)
1° aliphatic RNH2 + HNO2 → ROH + N2↑ + H2O (immediate N2 evolution)
1° aromatic ArNH2 + HNO2 (0-5°C) → ArN2+X− (stable diazonium salt)
2° amine R2NH + HNO2 → R2N-N=O (N-nitrosamine, yellow oil)
3° aromatic amine + HNO2 → p-nitroso derivative (ring substitution)
topics.worked_example: Distinguishing ethylamine, diethylamine, and triethylamine with HNO2 at 0-5°C: ethylamine (1°) shows brisk N2 evolution; diethylamine (2°) gives a yellow, oily N-nitrosamine layer; triethylamine (3°) simply dissolves as an unstable salt with no visible organic product.
common_mistakes: Assuming the carbylamine test also works for secondary and tertiary amines, rather than recognising it as diagnostic exclusively for primary amines.

Believing 1° aliphatic and 1° aromatic amines behave identically toward HNO2 at 0-5°C, when the aliphatic diazonium salt decomposes at once (N2 evolved) while the aromatic one is isolable/stable at that temperature.
Forgetting that tertiary AROMATIC amines still react with HNO2 (ring substitution to a p-nitroso product) even though tertiary ALIPHATIC amines give no characteristic organic product.

topics.name: Electrophilic Substitution in Aromatic Amines
topics.summary: The -NH2 group is one of the strongest activating, ortho/para-directing groups on a benzene ring, since its nitrogen lone pair conjugates directly into the ring, raising electron density especially at the ortho and para positions. This high reactivity causes practical problems: bromination of aniline with bromine water proceeds so readily that it does not stop at mono-substitution -- it directly gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline (white precipitate) without needing a Lewis-acid catalyst (unlike benzene, which needs one). To obtain a mono-substituted product, the amine is first acetylated (protected as acetanilide), which moderates -- without removing -- the ring-activating power by tying up part of the nitrogen lone pair in the amide's own resonance, allowing controlled mono-bromination (mainly para) before hydrolysis regenerates the free amine. Nitration is even more complicated: aniline is basic enough that, in the strongly acidic nitrating mixture (conc. HNO3/H2SO4), a significant fraction is protonated to the anilinium ion (-NH3+), which is an electron-withdrawing, META-directing group, so direct nitration of aniline gives a mixture of ortho, meta, and para nitroanilines with more meta product than -NH2 alone would predict; in practice, acetanilide is nitrated instead (predominantly para) and then hydrolyzed to obtain pure p-nitroaniline.
key_formulas: Aniline + 3Br2 (aq.) → 2,4,6-tribromoaniline↓ (white ppt) + 3HBr, no catalyst needed
Aniline --(CH3CO)2O--> acetanilide --Br2/CH3COOH--> p-bromoacetanilide --hydrolysis--> p-bromoaniline
Aniline + conc. HNO3/H2SO4 → o-, m-, p-nitroaniline (mixture; meta boosted by anilinium-ion formation)
topics.worked_example: To make pure p-bromoaniline: first acetylate aniline (→ acetanilide) to moderate ring activation, then brominate (para product dominates), then hydrolyze the amide back to the free amine -- direct bromination of aniline itself instead gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.
common_mistakes: Expecting bromination of aniline to need a Lewis-acid catalyst (as for benzene) and to stop cleanly at mono-substitution without any protecting step.
Assuming -NH2 remains purely an o,p-director/activator throughout nitration in strong acid, without accounting for significant protonation to -NH3+ (a meta-director/deactivator) in that medium.
Believing acetylation of aniline is done to switch its directing behaviour to meta, rather than to moderate (tone down) the same o,p-directing activation so that mono-substitution becomes achievable.

topics.name: Diazonium Salts: Preparation and Structure
topics.summary: A diazonium salt, general formula Ar-N2+X−, is made by diazotization: treating a primary aromatic amine with sodium nitrite and a mineral acid (usually HCl) at a low temperature of 0-5°C (an ice-salt bath is typical) -- above about 5°C the diazonium salt decomposes/hydrolyzes rapidly, so strict temperature control is essential. The nitrous acid needed is generated in situ from NaNO2 + HCl. Structurally, the diazonium group -N≡N+ is linear, with the formal positive charge located predominantly on the terminal nitrogen; the whole -C-N≡N group lies in (or close to) the plane of the aromatic ring. Diazonium salts are generally stable only in cold solution; the solid chlorides can be explosive on drying/heating, though some salts (e.g., tetrafluoroborates) are more stable as solids. Their key synthetic value is that the readily-lost N2 makes the diazonium group an excellent leaving group, enabling replacement of -NH2 by many other substituents that are otherwise difficult or impossible to introduce directly onto a benzene ring.
key_formulas: ArNH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl --0-5°C--> ArN2+Cl− + NaCl + 2H2O (diazotization)
Structure: Ar-N≡N+X− (linear -N2+ group, positive charge mainly on the terminal N)
topics.worked_example: Preparation of benzenediazonium chloride: aniline is dissolved in excess dilute HCl, cooled to 0-5°C in an ice-salt bath, and cold aqueous NaNO2 is added slowly with stirring, keeping the temperature below 5°C throughout, to give C6H5N2+Cl− in solution.
common_mistakes: Carrying out diazotization at room temperature (or letting the mixture warm) instead of maintaining 0-5°C, causing the diazonium salt to decompose before it can be used.
Attempting diazotization on a secondary or tertiary aromatic amine expecting a stable diazonium salt, when only a PRIMARY aromatic amine gives ArN2+ under these conditions.
Assuming diazonium salts are generally stable, easily isolable solids at room temperature, rather than species normally generated and used in situ, cold, in solution.

topics.name: Reactions of Diazonium Salts: Sandmeyer and Replacement Reactions
topics.summary: Because N2 is an excellent leaving group, a diazonium salt undergoes many substitution reactions in which -N2+ is replaced by a nucleophile, opening routes to aryl derivatives that are difficult to make by direct substitution on benzene. Sandmeyer reaction: cuprous halide (CuCl or CuBr) in the corresponding hydrohalic acid replaces -N2+ with -Cl or -Br (Ar-N2+ + CuCl/HCl → Ar-Cl + N2); a related route uses Cu powder + HX. Aryl iodides form more simply, WITHOUT any copper catalyst, just by treating the diazonium salt with KI. Aryl cyanides form with CuCN/KCN (also a Sandmeyer-type reaction), useful because -CN cannot otherwise be put directly onto an unactivated benzene ring. Boiling the diazonium salt with water hydrolyzes it to a phenol (Ar-OH) + N2 + acid. Treatment with H3PO2 (hypophosphorous acid) and water reduces the diazonium group away entirely, replacing -N2+ with -H (deamination) -- useful for removing an -NH2 group that was needed only to direct an earlier substitution and is deaminated away once its job is done.
key_formulas: ArN2+Cl− + CuCl/HCl → ArCl + N2 (Sandmeyer)
ArN2+Cl− + CuBr/HBr → ArBr + N2 (Sandmeyer)
ArN2+Cl− + KI → ArI + N2 + KCl (no Cu needed)
ArN2+Cl− + CuCN/KCN → ArCN + N2 (Sandmeyer)
ArN2+Cl− + H2O --Δ--> ArOH + N2 + HCl
ArN2+Cl− + H3PO2 + H2O → ArH + N2 + H3PO3 + HCl (deamination)
topics.worked_example: To make iodobenzene from aniline: diazotize aniline (NaNO2/HCl, 0-5°C) to get C6H5N2+Cl−, then simply add KI solution -- no copper catalyst required -- to obtain C6H5I + N2 + KCl directly.
common_mistakes: Adding a copper catalyst when preparing an aryl iodide from a diazonium salt, not realising KI alone effects the substitution, unlike the Cl/Br/CN Sandmeyer cases.
Confusing the hydrolysis product (phenol, from boiling with water) with the deamination product (arene, from H3PO2), since both remove the diazonium group but replace it with different atoms.

Assuming these replacement reactions could instead be achieved directly on a haloarene or unfunctionalized benzene ring, missing that diazonium chemistry is often the ONLY practical route to that substitution pattern.

topics.name: Coupling Reaction and Azo Dyes
topics.summary: Unlike the replacement reactions above, where the diazonium group is lost as N2, a coupling reaction retains both nitrogens: the diazonium ion acts as a weak electrophile and attacks a strongly activated aromatic ring (one bearing -OH or -NR2/-NH2), forming a new N=N (azo) linkage that bridges the two aromatic rings, Ar-N=N-Ar'. This electrophilic aromatic substitution occurs almost exclusively at the PARA position of the second, electron-rich ring relative to its activating group, unless that position is already blocked, in which case ortho coupling occurs instead. Classic examples: benzenediazonium chloride + phenol (in mildly alkaline solution, where phenol is partly present as the more nucleophilic phenoxide) gives p-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange solid; benzenediazonium chloride + N,N-dimethylaniline gives p-(dimethylamino)azobenzene, a yellow dye (the parent structure of the indicator methyl orange). These extensively conjugated azo compounds (Ar-N=N-Ar') absorb visible light strongly and are therefore intensely coloured, which is why azo coupling is the basis of a large class of synthetic azo dyes used in textiles and as acid-base indicators.
key_formulas: ArN2+Cl− + C6H5OH (mild base) → Ar-N=N-C6H4-OH-p (p-hydroxyazobenzene, orange)
ArN2+Cl− + C6H5N(CH3)2 → Ar-N=N-C6H4-N(CH3)2-p (p-(dimethylamino)azobenzene, yellow)
topics.worked_example: Benzenediazonium chloride coupled with phenol under mildly alkaline conditions attacks the phenol ring's para position (strongly activated by -O−/-OH) to give p-hydroxyazobenzene, C6H5-N=N-C6H4-OH; if the para position were already blocked, coupling would occur ortho to -OH instead.
common_mistakes: Confusing a coupling reaction (both aromatic rings retained, joined by -N=N-) with a replacement/Sandmeyer-type reaction (where N2 gas is lost and the ring's nitrogen substituent disappears entirely).
Assuming azo coupling can occur at any position of the activated ring, rather than recognising the strong preference for para (or ortho if para is blocked) relative to the activating -OH/-NR2 group.
Overlooking that the diazonium salt must stay cold and freshly prepared for coupling to succeed, since it decomposes on warming before it can react with the coupling partner.

topics.name: Distinguishing Tests for Amines: Hinsberg's Test
topics.summary: Hinsberg's test distinguishes primary, secondary, and tertiary amines using benzenesulfonyl chloride (C6H5SO2Cl, 'Hinsberg's reagent') together with KOH. A primary amine forms an N-alkyl(or aryl) benzenesulfonamide that still carries one N-H; because this remaining hydrogen is made distinctly acidic by the strongly electron-withdrawing adjacent -SO2- group, the sulfonamide dissolves in excess aqueous KOH as its potassium salt (a clear solution), and acidifying afterwards precipitates the free sulfonamide back out. A secondary amine forms an N,N-dialkyl benzenesulfonamide with NO N-H remaining (both positions on nitrogen are now substituted); lacking any acidic hydrogen, this product is insoluble in KOH and separates out directly as a solid/oil. A tertiary amine has no N-H to begin with, so it fails to react with benzenesulfonyl chloride at all; it may briefly form a salt with HCl generated in situ, but on adding excess KOH the free tertiary amine, being insoluble in the aqueous alkaline layer, simply separates out unchanged. This clean three-way solubility difference makes Hinsberg's test a reliable single experiment to classify an unknown amine, complementing the carbylamine test, which only flags primary amines.
key_formulas: 1°: RNH2 + C6H5SO2Cl → RNH-SO2C6H5 (has N-H, acidic) --KOH--> soluble salt
2°: R2NH + C6H5SO2Cl → R2N-SO2C6H5 (no N-H) -- insoluble in KOH
3°: R3N + C6H5SO2Cl → no reaction; R3N insoluble, separates unchanged in KOH layer
topics.worked_example: An unknown amine is treated with Hinsberg's reagent and KOH: a clear (dissolved) mixture indicates a primary amine; an insoluble sulfonamide precipitate indicates a secondary amine; an insoluble layer that is simply the unreacted starting amine indicates a tertiary amine.
common_mistakes: Assuming the secondary amine's sulfonamide product also dissolves in KOH like the primary one's does, forgetting it has no remaining acidic N-H once both nitrogen positions are substituted.

Believing a tertiary amine reacts with benzenesulfonyl chloride to form some insoluble sulfonamide, rather than recognising it simply fails to react at all (no N-H) and separates out as the unreacted free amine.
Confusing Hinsberg's test (distinguishes 1°/2°/3° from one another) with the carbylamine test (only flags primary vs. non-primary amines).

questions.question: Which of the following is a secondary (2°) amine?
options: (CH3)3N
CH3-NH-CH3
C6H5NH2
CH3CH2NH2
questions.explanation: Nitrogen carries two methyl groups and one H, i.e., two C-N bonds, which makes this dimethylamine, a secondary amine.
questions.hint: Count the number of carbon groups directly bonded to the nitrogen atom.
distractor_logic: This has three alkyl groups on nitrogen (three C-N bonds), so it is a tertiary amine, not secondary.
Aniline has only one group (the ring) on nitrogen, so it is a primary aromatic amine, not secondary.
This has only one alkyl group on nitrogen (one C-N bond), so it is a primary amine, not secondary.

questions.question: The hybridization of the nitrogen atom in a simple aliphatic amine such as CH3NH2 is:
options: sp3
dsp2
sp2
sp
questions.explanation: Like ammonia, the nitrogen in an aliphatic amine is sp3 hybridized and pyramidal, with one hybrid orbital holding the lone pair.
questions.hint: Compare the shape of an amine's nitrogen with that of ammonia.
distractor_logic: Nitrogen does not use d orbitals in ordinary bonding, so this hybridization state is not applicable here.
sp2 nitrogen with a flattened, partly planar lone pair is more characteristic of an amide nitrogen or an aromatic amine's resonance-delocalized nitrogen, not a simple aliphatic amine.
sp hybridization describes linear systems such as the nitrogen in a nitrile or a diazonium salt, not the pyramidal nitrogen of an aliphatic amine.

questions.question: Amines are classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary based on:
options: the type of carbon (1°, 2°, 3°) to which the -NH2 group is attached
the total number of carbon atoms in the molecule
whether the amine is a gas, liquid, or solid at room temperature
the number of hydrogen atoms of ammonia that have been replaced by alkyl/aryl groups
questions.explanation: This is the defining rule for amine classification, based on how many N-H bonds of NH3 have been substituted.
questions.hint: Recall how this classification differs from the one used for alcohols.
distractor_logic: That rule is used to classify alcohols and alkyl halides, not amines, which are classified by substitution at nitrogen instead.
Chain length or total carbon count has no bearing on whether an amine is primary, secondary, or tertiary.
Physical state depends on molar mass and intermolecular forces, not on the structural classification of the amine.

questions.question: The IUPAC name of CH3-CH2-NH2 is:
options: Ethylamine
Aminoethane
Ethanamine
Ethanamide
questions.explanation: The terminal '-e' of ethane is replaced with '-amine' to give the IUPAC substitutive name ethanamine.
questions.hint: Drop the final 'e' of the alkane name and add the amine suffix.
distractor_logic: This is the common (trivial) name built from the alkyl-group name plus 'amine', not the IUPAC substitutive name.
This incorrectly uses 'amino' as a prefix on the parent hydride name instead of the correct '-amine' suffix substitution used for the principal amine group.
This names the corresponding carboxamide, CH3CONH2 -- a completely different functional group (amide, not amine).

questions.question: The IUPAC name of C6H5-NH-CH3 is:
options: o-Toluidine
N-methylaniline
Benzylamine
N,N-dimethylaniline
questions.explanation: The larger group (the ring) is kept as the aniline parent, and the methyl group on nitrogen is cited with the italic N-locant.
questions.hint: Decide whether the methyl group sits on the ring or directly on the nitrogen.
distractor_logic: This is a ring-substituted isomer (methyl attached to a ring carbon), a structurally different primary aromatic amine, not an N-substituted aniline.
This is C6H5CH2NH2, where a -CH2- group links the ring to nitrogen -- a different compound from one with the methyl directly on the ring nitrogen.
This compound would need two methyl groups on nitrogen, but the given structure has only one.

questions.question: In amine nomenclature, a substituent attached to the nitrogen atom (rather than to the carbon chain) is indicated using:
options: Greek letters such as α, β
an italic capital N- locant, e.g., N-methyl-
the prefix 'iso-'
numbered locants such as 2- or 3-
questions.explanation: The italic N-locant is the standard way IUPAC nomenclature shows that a substituent sits on the amine nitrogen rather than on a numbered carbon.
questions.hint: Think of how N,N-dimethylaniline signals that both methyls sit on nitrogen.
distractor_logic: Greek-letter labelling is used in some older naming conventions for carbon positions relative to a functional group, not for nitrogen substitution in amine names.
'Iso-' denotes a branched carbon-skeleton pattern and has nothing to do with indicating substitution on nitrogen.
Numbered locants refer to positions on the carbon chain or ring, not to the nitrogen atom.

questions.question: Ammonolysis of ethyl bromide with excess ammonia in a sealed tube mainly suffers from the problem of:
options: bromide being too poor a leaving group for the substitution to occur
the product being exclusively an aromatic amine
further alkylation of the primary amine formed, giving a mixture of secondary and tertiary amines plus a quaternary ammonium salt
the reaction not proceeding at all under sealed-tube heating conditions
questions.explanation: The primary amine product is itself nucleophilic and keeps reacting with more alkyl halide, so a mixture of products results rather than one pure amine.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the primary amine once it is formed in the same pot.
distractor_logic: Bromide is actually a good leaving group, and this SN2-type substitution proceeds readily; that is not the limitation here.
Ethyl bromide is an aliphatic halide, so only aliphatic amine products form; no aromatic amine is involved.
Ammonolysis does proceed readily under these conditions; the problem is over-alkylation, not a lack of reaction.

questions.question: Aniline is manufactured industrially mainly by:
options: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis using bromobenzene
reduction of benzonitrile (C6H5CN) with LiAlH4
catalytic hydrogenation (or Fe/HCl reduction) of nitrobenzene
ammonolysis of chlorobenzene with excess ammonia
questions.explanation: Reduction of the readily available nitrobenzene is the standard, direct industrial route to aniline.
questions.hint: Which starting material already has the nitrogen attached directly to the ring?
distractor_logic: Aryl halides cannot undergo the nucleophilic substitution step with phthalimide anion that this method requires, so it cannot give aniline.
This reduces the nitrile to benzylamine, C6H5CH2NH2 (the CN carbon is retained as a CH2 group), not to aniline.
Aryl halides resist nucleophilic substitution under ordinary conditions, so this is not a practical or industrial route to aniline.

questions.question: Treating propanenitrile, CH3CH2CN, with LiAlH4 gives:
options: CH3CH2CONH2 (propanamide)
CH3CH2NH2 (ethanamine)
CH3CH2CH2NH2 (propan-1-amine)
CH3CH2COOH (propanoic acid)
questions.explanation: LiAlH4 fully reduces the C≡N triple bond to a -CH2-NH2 group without removing any carbon, so all three carbons of the nitrile are retained in the amine.
questions.hint: LiAlH4 reduces the triple bond fully to single bonds, adding hydrogens without touching the carbon count.
distractor_logic: This is only a partial hydrolysis product of the nitrile, not the fully reduced product obtained with LiAlH4.
This would mean losing a carbon during reduction, but the nitrile carbon itself becomes the -CH2NH2 carbon of the product, so no carbon is lost.
This is an oxidation/hydrolysis product of a nitrile, not what LiAlH4 (a reducing agent) produces.

questions.question: Reductive amination of acetone, CH3COCH3, with NH3 in the presence of H2/Ni gives:
options: isopropanol, (CH3)2CHOH
acetone oxime, CH3C(=NOH)CH3
isopropylamine, (CH3)2CHNH2
n-propylamine, CH3CH2CH2NH2
questions.explanation: The carbonyl carbon of acetone is converted to a CH-NH2 carbon, carrying over the branching pattern already present in the ketone.
questions.hint: The branching of the ketone's carbon skeleton carries over into the amine product.
distractor_logic: This is simple catalytic hydrogenation of the C=O bond with no nitrogen incorporation at all, i.e., reduction without amination.
This is the product of acetone with hydroxylamine (NH2OH), not the reductive amination product formed with NH3/H2/Ni.
This unbranched product would come from reductive amination of propanal, not from the branched ketone acetone.

questions.topic: Gabriel Synthesis and Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation
questions.question: In the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis, treating phthalimide with ethanolic KOH serves to:
options: directly alkylate phthalimide with an alkyl halide
generate the potassium salt of phthalimide, providing a nucleophilic nitrogen for subsequent alkylation
reduce phthalimide's carbonyl groups
hydrolyze phthalimide completely to phthalic acid and ammonia
questions.explanation: KOH deprotonates the acidic imide N-H (made acidic by the two flanking carbonyls), producing a nucleophile ready to be alkylated.
questions.hint: Think about what KOH, a base, would do to an acidic N-H.
distractor_logic: KOH alone does not add an alkyl group; it only deprotonates the N-H. Alkylation requires a separate step with an alkyl halide.
KOH is a base, not a reducing agent; the two carbonyl groups are untouched at this step.
That hydrolysis happens in the LAST step of the synthesis, on the N-alkylphthalimide, not on phthalimide itself at this early stage.

questions.topic: Gabriel Synthesis and Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation
questions.question: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis cannot be used to directly prepare aniline because:
options: the hydrolysis step destroys aromatic rings
phthalimide reacts explosively with aromatic compounds
aryl halides do not undergo the nucleophilic substitution required with the phthalimide anion
aniline is too basic to be formed by this method
questions.explanation: The alkylation step of this synthesis needs an SN2-type substitution, which aryl halides cannot undergo under these conditions.
questions.hint: Which step of the synthesis needs a good SN2 substrate?
distractor_logic: Acidic or alkaline hydrolysis of the phthalimide portion does not affect an aromatic ring attached elsewhere in the molecule.
There is no such hazard; this is not the actual reason the method fails for aromatic amines.
The basicity of the eventual product is not the limiting factor; the limitation is purely mechanistic, at the alkylation step.

questions.topic: Gabriel Synthesis and Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation
questions.question: Hoffmann bromamide degradation converts a primary amide, RCONH2, into an amine with:
options: one carbon atom fewer than the starting amide, since the carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate/CO2
one carbon atom more than the starting amide
two carbon atoms fewer than the starting amide
exactly the same number of carbon atoms as the starting amide
questions.explanation: The rearrangement removes the carbonyl carbon entirely, leaving RNH2 with one less carbon than RCONH2.
questions.hint: Recall what 'degradation' implies about the carbon count of the product.
distractor_logic: This is a degradation reaction, meaning loss (not gain) of one carbon from the starting amide.
Only the single carbonyl carbon is lost in this reaction, not two carbons.
One specific carbon, the original carbonyl carbon, is lost as carbonate during the rearrangement, so the carbon count does change.

questions.question: At room temperature, methylamine, dimethylamine, and trimethylamine typically exist as:
options: gases with a fishy/ammonia-like smell
colorless, odorless liquids
highly viscous oils
crystalline solids
questions.explanation: These three small amines are gases at room temperature and share a characteristic pungent, fish-like or ammonia-like odor.
questions.hint: Recall the state of matter and characteristic smell of the smallest amines.
distractor_logic: They are gases (not liquids) at room temperature, and they are certainly not odorless -- they have a distinctive smell.
These lower amines are gases at room temperature, not oils.
Only much higher (longer-chain) amines are solids; these small amines are gases at room temperature.

questions.question: Among the isomeric C3H9N amines 1-propanamine (1°), N-methylethanamine (2°), and trimethylamine (3°), the one with the HIGHEST boiling point is:
options: 1-propanamine
N-methylethanamine
all three have identical boiling points
trimethylamine
questions.explanation: As a primary amine it has two N-H bonds available for intermolecular hydrogen bonding, more than either of the other two isomers.
questions.hint: Count how many N-H bonds are available for hydrogen bonding in each isomer.
distractor_logic: As a secondary amine it has only one N-H bond, fewer hydrogen-bond donors than the primary isomer, so its boiling point is lower.
They differ measurably in boiling point because of the differing extents of intermolecular hydrogen bonding each can form.
As a tertiary amine it has no N-H bonds at all, giving it the LOWEST boiling point of the three, not the highest.

questions.question: Primary amines have lower boiling points than alcohols of comparable molecular mass mainly because:
options: amines cannot form hydrogen bonds at all, unlike alcohols
amines are always more branched than alcohols, which lowers their boiling point
nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so N-H···N hydrogen bonds are weaker than O-H···O hydrogen bonds
amines always have a lower molecular mass than the corresponding alcohols
questions.explanation: The weaker intermolecular hydrogen bonding in amines, arising from nitrogen's lower electronegativity relative to oxygen, gives them lower boiling points than comparable alcohols.
questions.hint: Compare the electronegativities of nitrogen and oxygen.
distractor_logic: Primary and secondary amines DO form hydrogen bonds via N-H, just weaker ones than the O-H bonds in alcohols; they are not entirely absent.
Branching is not a defining structural difference between amines and alcohols in general, and it is not the underlying cause of this boiling-point difference.
The comparison here is specifically for compounds of similar molecular mass, so a mass difference is not the explanation.

questions.question: Amines behave as bases mainly because:
options: nitrogen carries a partial negative charge purely due to its electronegativity, with no lone pair involved
nitrogen carries a lone pair of electrons that can accept a proton
amines contain an acidic N-H bond that ionizes to release H+
the carbon skeleton attached to nitrogen is electron-withdrawing
questions.explanation: The available, unshared lone pair on nitrogen is exactly what allows an amine to accept a proton (or donate to a Lewis acid), making it basic.
questions.hint: What feature of nitrogen allows it to accept H+?
distractor_logic: The key basicity-conferring feature is specifically the available LONE PAIR on nitrogen, not simply its electronegativity.
That description is of acidic behavior, which is not why amines are basic.
Alkyl groups are actually electron-DONATING by the inductive effect, which increases basicity, not electron-withdrawing.

questions.question: In the gas phase (no solvent effects), the basicity order of methyl-substituted amines and ammonia is:
options: CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > (CH3)2NH > NH3
NH3 > CH3NH2 > (CH3)2NH > (CH3)3N
(CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3
(CH3)3N > (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > NH3
questions.explanation: In the gas phase, basicity tracks the pure inductive (+I) electron-donating effect of the methyl groups, which increases steadily with more substitution.
questions.hint: Without solvent, only the electron-donating inductive effect of the methyl groups matters.
distractor_logic: This ordering does not follow a consistent inductive or solvation trend.
This reverses the actual trend; alkyl substitution's +I effect should increase, not decrease, basicity relative to ammonia.
This is the AQUEOUS-solution order, reflecting solvation of the ammonium cation; it is not the pure gas-phase order.

questions.question: Aniline is a weaker base than ammonia mainly because:
options: aniline's nitrogen has no lone pair at all
aniline is a solid at room temperature while ammonia is a gas, and solids are always weaker bases
the nitrogen lone pair in aniline is delocalized into the benzene ring by resonance, making it less available to accept a proton
the benzene ring withdraws electron density from nitrogen purely by an inductive effect
questions.explanation: Conjugation of the lone pair into the aromatic ring reduces its availability for protonation, lowering aniline's basicity relative to ammonia.
questions.hint: Think about what the ring can do to the nitrogen lone pair through conjugation.
distractor_logic: Aniline's nitrogen still has a lone pair; it is merely less available for protonation, not absent.
Physical state at room temperature has no bearing on intrinsic basicity.
The dominant effect here is RESONANCE delocalization of the lone pair, not a simple inductive withdrawal.

questions.topic: Acylation and Alkylation Reactions of Amines
questions.question: Acetylation of aniline with acetic anhydride (a trace of pyridine present) gives:
options: acetanilide, C6H5NHCOCH3
p-aminoacetophenone
aniline hydrochloride, C6H5NH3+Cl−
N,N-diacetylaniline
questions.explanation: One of aniline's two N-H hydrogens is replaced by an acetyl group, giving the N-substituted amide acetanilide.
questions.hint: Acetic anhydride reacts at the nitrogen, replacing one N-H.
distractor_logic: This would result from Friedel-Crafts acylation of the ring carbon, not from N-acylation of the amine group.
This is a simple acid-base salt formed with HCl, not the acylation product obtained with acetic anhydride.
Only one N-H is available for acylation on aniline's primary amine nitrogen once mono-acylation occurs, so only mono-acetylation is possible.

questions.topic: Acylation and Alkylation Reactions of Amines
questions.question: A tertiary amine does NOT undergo the typical acylation reaction with acetyl chloride to form an amide because:
options: it has no N-H hydrogen available to be replaced by the acyl group
tertiary amines decompose on contact with acid chlorides
tertiary amines are too unreactive/non-nucleophilic to approach the acyl chloride at all
acetyl chloride only reacts with aromatic amines
questions.explanation: Acylation replaces an N-H bond with an acyl group; a tertiary amine simply has none to replace.
questions.hint: What does acylation actually replace on the nitrogen atom?
distractor_logic: No such decomposition occurs; a tertiary amine may form a transient salt or act catalytically, but it does not decompose.
Tertiary amines remain good nucleophiles/bases; the issue is purely structural (the absence of N-H), not a lack of nucleophilicity.
Acetyl chloride reacts with aliphatic 1°/2° amines too, whenever an N-H is present, regardless of whether the amine is aliphatic or aromatic.

questions.topic: Acylation and Alkylation Reactions of Amines
questions.question: Successive treatment of a primary amine with excess alkyl halide (alkylation) eventually leads to the formation of:
options: an amide
a stable secondary amine only, with no further reaction
a quaternary ammonium salt, R4N+X−
an isocyanide
questions.explanation: Each product amine remains nucleophilic and keeps reacting with more alkyl halide until all four positions on nitrogen are alkylated, giving a quaternary salt.
questions.hint: Does the reaction stop once a secondary or tertiary amine has formed?
distractor_logic: Alkylation with alkyl halides forms C-N bonds directly; forming an amide would require reaction with an acyl chloride/anhydride instead.
The secondary amine formed is itself still nucleophilic and continues reacting with more alkyl halide, so the reaction does not stop there.
Isocyanides form specifically from primary amines treated with CHCl3/alcoholic KOH (the carbylamine reaction), not from simple alkylation with alkyl halides.

questions.topic: Carbylamine Reaction and Reaction with Nitrous Acid
questions.question: The carbylamine (isocyanide) test, using CHCl3 and alcoholic KOH, gives a foul-smelling product specifically with:
options: all amines regardless of class
secondary amines only
tertiary amines only
primary amines (both aliphatic and aromatic)
questions.explanation: Only primary amines have the structural requirement to form an isocyanide in this reaction, regardless of whether they are aliphatic or aromatic.
questions.hint: This test is used specifically to identify one class of amine.
distractor_logic: The test is specifically diagnostic for primary amines; secondary and tertiary amines give no reaction.
Secondary amines give no isocyanide product in this test at all.
Tertiary amines also give no reaction in this test, since they lack the N-H the mechanism requires.

questions.topic: Carbylamine Reaction and Reaction with Nitrous Acid
questions.question: When a primary ALIPHATIC amine reacts with nitrous acid (NaNO2/HCl) at 0-5°C, the immediately observable result is:
options: brisk evolution of nitrogen gas, as the unstable aliphatic diazonium salt decomposes at once
formation of a stable, isolable diazonium salt
formation of a yellow, oily nitrosamine
no visible reaction at all
questions.explanation: Aliphatic diazonium salts are far too unstable to survive, even in the cold, and decompose immediately with visible gas evolution.
questions.hint: Aliphatic and aromatic diazonium salts behave very differently at 0-5°C.
distractor_logic: Unlike aromatic diazonium salts, aliphatic diazonium salts are too unstable to isolate even at 0-5°C.
That product forms from SECONDARY amines reacting with HNO2, not from primary amines.
There is a clearly visible reaction -- vigorous gas evolution -- with primary aliphatic amines under these conditions.

questions.topic: Carbylamine Reaction and Reaction with Nitrous Acid
questions.question: A secondary amine, R2NH, reacts with nitrous acid to form:
options: a stable diazonium salt
no reaction at all
an N-nitrosamine, R2N-N=O, a yellow oily liquid
an isocyanide
questions.explanation: This is the characteristic product formed when a secondary amine's N-H reacts with nitrous acid.
questions.hint: Recall the specific colored, oily product characteristic of secondary amines here.
distractor_logic: Diazonium salt formation requires a PRIMARY amine; a secondary amine cannot form this product, since it lacks the second N-H the diazotization mechanism needs.
Secondary amines do react with HNO2, giving the characteristic nitrosamine product described above.
Isocyanides form from primary amines reacting with CHCl3/alcoholic KOH, an entirely different reagent and reaction.

questions.question: Aniline reacts with bromine water (no catalyst) to directly give:
options: p-bromoaniline only, as the sole mono-substituted product
2,4,6-tribromoaniline (white precipitate)
m-bromoaniline
bromobenzene
questions.explanation: The ring is so strongly activated by -NH2 that bromination proceeds all the way to the tri-substituted product without stopping at mono-substitution.
questions.hint: How strongly does -NH2 activate the ring compared with other substituents?
distractor_logic: Aniline's ring is activated too strongly for bromination to stop at mono-substitution without a protecting step first.
-NH2 is an ortho/para director, not a meta director, so meta substitution is not favored here.
This product would have lost the amino group entirely, which does not happen in this substitution reaction.

questions.question: -NH2 is a strongly activating, ortho/para-directing group on a benzene ring mainly because:
options: -NH2 has no lone pair available to interact with the ring
-NH2 physically blocks the ortho and para positions sterically, forcing substitution there
nitrogen is more electronegative than carbon and withdraws electron density inductively from the ring
the nitrogen lone pair conjugates (delocalizes) into the ring, increasing electron density especially at the ortho and para positions
questions.explanation: Resonance donation of the lone pair into the ring is the key electronic effect behind -NH2's strong activation and ortho/para direction.
questions.hint: Consider how the nitrogen lone pair can interact electronically with the ring.
distractor_logic: It is precisely because there IS a lone pair capable of resonance donation that -NH2 is so strongly activating.
The actual reason is electronic/resonance-based, not a steric-blocking effect.
While nitrogen is somewhat electronegative, the dominant, overriding effect on the ring is electron-donating resonance, not inductive withdrawal.

questions.question: Direct nitration of aniline with conc. HNO3/H2SO4 gives a significant amount of the meta isomer (in addition to ortho/para) mainly because:
options: the nitro group, once formed, directs further nitration to give more meta product
-NH2 is intrinsically a meta director under all conditions
nitric acid selectively attacks the meta position of all aromatic rings
in the strongly acidic medium, a substantial fraction of aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion (-NH3+), which is a meta-directing, deactivating group
questions.explanation: Protonation converts the strong o,p-director -NH2 into the meta-directing -NH3+ group for a significant fraction of the molecules present.
questions.hint: What happens to a basic -NH2 group in a strongly acidic nitrating mixture?
distractor_logic: This describes directing effects for a SECOND nitration step, not why meta product forms during the nitration of aniline itself.
Unprotonated -NH2 is an ortho/para director; the meta product arises specifically because of protonation in this strongly acidic medium.
Nitration has no inherent bias toward the meta position; the position attacked depends entirely on the substituents present on the ring.

questions.question: Diazotization of a primary aromatic amine requires reaction with:
options: acetic anhydride and pyridine
alcoholic KOH and CHCl3
NaNO2 and a mineral acid (e.g., HCl), at 0-5°C
Br2 and NaOH
questions.explanation: These are exactly the reagents and conditions needed to generate nitrous acid in situ and convert a primary aromatic amine into its diazonium salt.
questions.hint: Recall what generates nitrous acid in situ.
distractor_logic: These reagents perform N-acylation, not diazotization.
These are the reagents for the carbylamine test, unrelated to diazotization.
These reagents perform Hoffmann bromamide degradation on an amide, not diazotization of an amine.

questions.question: Diazotization must be carried out at 0-5°C because:
options: the aromatic amine itself decomposes above 5°C before it can react
higher temperature would prevent the amine from reacting with nitrous acid at all
NaNO2 does not dissolve in water below 5°C, so a higher temperature is normally needed instead
above this temperature the diazonium salt rapidly decomposes/hydrolyzes
questions.explanation: The diazonium PRODUCT is thermally unstable, so low temperature is essential to prevent its decomposition before use.
questions.hint: Which species -- starting material or product -- is thermally unstable here?
distractor_logic: It is the diazonium PRODUCT, not the starting amine, that is thermally unstable.
The amine would still react with HNO2 at higher temperature; the actual problem is that the diazonium product would not survive, not that the reaction wouldn't occur.
This reverses the actual logic: LOW temperature is required for the reaction to succeed, not avoided.

questions.question: The general structure of a diazonium salt is best represented as:
options: Ar-N≡N+X− (a linear -N2+ group attached to the aromatic ring)
Ar-N=N-Ar'
Ar-NO2
Ar-NH-NH2
questions.explanation: This linear diazonium group, with the terminal nitrogen carrying the formal positive charge, is the defining structural feature of a diazonium salt.
questions.hint: The diazonium group contains two nitrogen atoms in a specific linear arrangement.
distractor_logic: This represents an azo compound -- the COUPLING product of a diazonium salt with another aromatic ring, not the diazonium salt itself.
This represents a nitro compound, a completely different functional group from a diazonium salt.
This represents a hydrazine derivative, an entirely different functional group from a diazonium salt.

questions.topic: Reactions of Diazonium Salts: Sandmeyer and Replacement Reactions
questions.question: Treating benzenediazonium chloride with CuCl in the presence of HCl (Sandmeyer reaction) gives:
options: aniline, C6H5NH2
phenol, C6H5OH
bromobenzene, C6H5Br
chlorobenzene, C6H5Cl
questions.explanation: Cuprous chloride in HCl replaces the diazonium group with -Cl, a classic Sandmeyer substitution.
questions.hint: Which halide does CuCl/HCl deliver to the ring?
distractor_logic: Regenerating the amine would require reduction/deamination with H3PO2 (replacing -N2+ with -H), not a Sandmeyer halogenation.
Phenol forms from hydrolysis with plain WATER, not from the CuCl/HCl combination.
Bromobenzene requires CuBr/HBr, not CuCl/HCl.

questions.topic: Reactions of Diazonium Salts: Sandmeyer and Replacement Reactions
questions.question: Which reagent converts a diazonium salt into the corresponding aryl iodide WITHOUT needing a copper catalyst?
options: CuI
H2O
H3PO2
KI (potassium iodide)
questions.explanation: Unlike the Cl/Br/CN Sandmeyer substitutions, iodination of a diazonium salt proceeds directly with simple KI, no copper catalyst required.
questions.hint: Iodination is the one Sandmeyer-type substitution that skips the copper catalyst.
distractor_logic: While copper(I) salts mediate the Cl/Br/CN Sandmeyer substitutions, the iodide substitution proceeds directly with KI alone; copper is not needed.
This reagent hydrolyzes the diazonium salt to phenol, not to an aryl iodide.
This reagent performs deamination (replacement of -N2+ by -H), not iodination.

questions.topic: Reactions of Diazonium Salts: Sandmeyer and Replacement Reactions
questions.question: Boiling a diazonium salt solution with water gives:
options: an aromatic amine (regenerating the original starting material)
an aryl halide
a phenol
an azo dye
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis of the diazonium group by water replaces -N2+ with -OH, giving the corresponding phenol.
questions.hint: Water acts as the nucleophile that replaces the diazonium group here.
distractor_logic: Hydrolysis with water does not regenerate the amine; it replaces -N2+ with -OH, giving a phenol instead.
Aryl halides need a specific halide-donating reagent, such as CuCl/CuBr/KI, not plain water.
Azo dye formation requires coupling with a second, activated aromatic ring, not simple hydrolysis with water.

questions.question: A coupling reaction between a diazonium salt and phenol (in mildly alkaline solution) gives:
options: chlorobenzene, with loss of N2 gas
a simple ether linking the two rings
two separate, unconnected aromatic rings
an azo compound (p-hydroxyazobenzene), retaining both nitrogen atoms as an -N=N- linkage
questions.explanation: Coupling reactions retain both nitrogens of the diazonium group, joining the two aromatic rings through a new -N=N- bond.
questions.hint: Does a coupling reaction lose nitrogen gas, like a Sandmeyer reaction does?
distractor_logic: That is a Sandmeyer-type replacement reaction product; in a coupling reaction, N2 is NOT lost.
No ether forms; the new bond created is an azo (-N=N-) linkage, not a C-O-C ether linkage.
Coupling specifically JOINS the two rings together via a new -N=N- bond, so they do not remain unconnected.

questions.question: Coupling of a diazonium salt with an activated aromatic ring (bearing -OH or -NR2) occurs predominantly at the:
options: ipso position, directly replacing the activating group
any position, with completely equal probability
meta position exclusively
para position of the second ring (or ortho if para is blocked)
questions.explanation: The strongly activating -OH/-NR2 group directs the incoming electrophile mainly to the para position, or ortho if para is unavailable.
questions.hint: Recall the directing effect of -OH or -NR2 groups in electrophilic substitution.
distractor_logic: The activating -OH/-NR2 group is retained; the new bond forms elsewhere on the ring, not by displacing the activating group.
There is a strong regiochemical preference dictated by the directing effect of the activating group, not random substitution.
Strongly activating -OH/-NR2 groups are ortho/para directors, so coupling occurs there, not at the meta position.

questions.question: Azo compounds such as p-(dimethylamino)azobenzene are intensely colored mainly because:
options: extended conjugation across the -N=N- linkage and both aromatic rings allows strong absorption of visible light
the compounds are radioactive, and radioactive decay produces visible light
they are always strongly acidic, and acidic compounds are inherently colored
they contain nitrogen, and all nitrogen-containing organic compounds are colored
questions.explanation: The extensively conjugated azo chromophore absorbs strongly in the visible region, which is why these compounds appear intensely colored.
questions.hint: Think about what a long conjugated system does to visible-light absorption.
distractor_logic: There is no radioactivity involved in ordinary azo dyes; the color arises from electronic transitions in the conjugated system.
Acidity is unrelated to visible color; many colored compounds are neutral or basic, and many acids are colorless.
Most nitrogen compounds, such as simple amines, are colorless; nitrogen alone does not cause color.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Amines: Hinsberg's Test
questions.question: In Hinsberg's test, the reagent used to distinguish primary, secondary, and tertiary amines is:
options: nitrous acid (NaNO2/HCl)
chloroform and alcoholic KOH
benzenesulfonyl chloride, C6H5SO2Cl, together with KOH
acetic anhydride and pyridine
questions.explanation: This reagent combination is the defining feature of Hinsberg's test, giving characteristically different solubility behavior for each class of amine.
questions.hint: Recall the name of the sulfonyl chloride reagent used in this classic test.
distractor_logic: While HNO2 does give different products for 1°/2°/3° amines, 'Hinsberg's test' specifically refers to the benzenesulfonyl chloride/KOH procedure.
This combination is the carbylamine test reagent, which only detects primary amines, not a three-way distinguishing test.
This combination performs simple acylation of 1°/2° amines, and does not give the differential solubility behavior needed to distinguish all three classes.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Amines: Hinsberg's Test
questions.question: In Hinsberg's test, a PRIMARY amine's reaction product with benzenesulfonyl chloride:
options: does not form at all, since primary amines don't react with this reagent
dissolves in excess KOH, because the remaining N-H is rendered acidic by the adjacent -SO2- group
precipitates immediately and stays insoluble in KOH
evolves nitrogen gas
questions.explanation: The N-alkylbenzenesulfonamide formed still has one acidic N-H, which lets it dissolve as a potassium salt in excess KOH.
questions.hint: Does the primary amine's sulfonamide product still have an acidic N-H?
distractor_logic: Primary amines DO react readily with benzenesulfonyl chloride, forming a sulfonamide with one N-H remaining.
That behavior describes the SECONDARY amine's product, which has no acidic N-H left after both nitrogen positions are substituted.
Gas evolution is characteristic of the HNO2/diazonium test on 1° aliphatic amines, not of the Hinsberg benzenesulfonyl chloride reaction.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Amines: Hinsberg's Test
questions.question: A tertiary amine, when subjected to Hinsberg's test, is observed to:
options: not react with benzenesulfonyl chloride (no N-H available) and separate out as the free, insoluble amine after adding KOH
decompose completely, releasing ammonia gas
form a sulfonamide that precipitates as an insoluble solid, just like a secondary amine's product
form a sulfonamide that dissolves in KOH, just like a primary amine's product
questions.explanation: With no N-H to react, the tertiary amine is chemically untouched by the sulfonyl chloride and simply remains insoluble as itself once KOH is added.
questions.hint: Does a tertiary amine have an N-H for the sulfonyl chloride to react with?
distractor_logic: No decomposition of this type occurs; the amine simply fails to react and remains chemically unchanged.
A tertiary amine has no N-H to react with the sulfonyl chloride in the first place, so no sulfonamide of any kind is formed.
That solubility behavior is characteristic of the PRIMARY amine's product, not the tertiary amine, which does not react at all.

questions.question: Which of the following classification statements is CORRECT?
options: (CH3)3C-NH2 is classified as a primary amine, even though the carbon bearing the -NH2 group is tertiary
Diphenylamine, C6H5-NH-C6H5, is classified as a tertiary amine
(CH3)3C-NH2 is classified as a tertiary amine, since it is attached to a tertiary carbon
N,N-dimethylaniline is classified as a secondary amine
questions.explanation: Amine classification depends only on the number of carbon groups attached directly to nitrogen (here, one), regardless of what type of carbon that group is.
questions.hint: Amine classification always counts groups on nitrogen, never the type of carbon involved.
distractor_logic: Diphenylamine's nitrogen carries two aryl groups plus one H (two C-N bonds), making it a secondary amine, not tertiary.
This wrongly applies the alcohol/halide classification rule (based on the attached carbon) to an amine, which is instead classified by substitution at nitrogen.
N,N-dimethylaniline's nitrogen carries the ring plus two methyl groups (three C-N bonds), making it a tertiary amine, not secondary.

questions.question: The total number of structurally distinct amines (primary + secondary + tertiary) possible with molecular formula C3H9N is:
questions.explanation: There are two primary amines (propan-1-amine and propan-2-amine), one secondary amine (N-methylethanamine), and one tertiary amine (trimethylamine) -- four isomers in total.
questions.hint: Systematically list the primary, then secondary, then tertiary possibilities for 3 carbons and 1 nitrogen.
distractor_logic: This overcounts; no fifth structurally distinct amine is possible with this molecular formula.
This undercounts by missing one of the isomers, typically one of the two primary amines (propan-1-amine or propan-2-amine).
This counts only the primary amines and forgets the secondary (N-methylethanamine) and tertiary (trimethylamine) isomers entirely.

questions.question: A tertiary amine bearing three different groups on nitrogen (plus a lone pair) is technically a stereocenter, yet stable enantiomers of such amines cannot usually be isolated at room temperature. This is because:
options: rapid pyramidal inversion at nitrogen, through a planar sp2 transition state, interconverts the two configurations far faster than they can be separated
the lone pair on nitrogen is not stereochemically significant and can be ignored when assessing chirality
amines with three different alkyl groups on nitrogen do not exist structurally
the nitrogen atom in amines is never a stereocenter, regardless of the three substituents
questions.explanation: The energy barrier to pyramidal inversion at nitrogen is low enough that the two mirror-image forms interconvert too quickly to be isolated as separate enantiomers.
questions.hint: Consider the shape nitrogen must pass through as it 'flips' from one pyramidal form to the other.
distractor_logic: The lone pair does occupy a definite spatial position and is relevant to why the molecule is momentarily pyramidal/chiral; it is fast inversion, not the lone pair's irrelevance, that prevents isolation.
Such tertiary amines certainly exist (e.g., N-ethyl-N-methylpropan-1-amine); this is not the reason enantiomers can't be isolated.
With three different groups plus a lone pair, nitrogen genuinely is a stereocenter at any instant; the issue is that rapid inversion prevents isolation, not the absence of a stereocenter.

questions.question: The correct IUPAC name of CH3-CH2-CH2-NH-CH3 is:
options: N-propylmethanamine
2-methylpropan-1-amine
N,N-dimethylpropan-1-amine
N-methylpropan-1-amine
questions.explanation: The larger group on nitrogen (the propyl chain) is chosen as the parent 'propan-1-amine', and the smaller methyl group on nitrogen is cited with the italic N-locant.
questions.hint: Which group attached to nitrogen -- propyl or methyl -- is larger, and should therefore be the parent chain?
distractor_logic: This has the parent/substituent choice backwards: the larger group (propyl) should be the parent chain, not cited as an N-substituent on a 'methanamine' parent.
This numbered locant implies the methyl group is on carbon-2 of the propyl chain, not on the nitrogen atom, which misrepresents the actual structure.
This compound would need two methyl groups on nitrogen, but only one methyl group is present on nitrogen here.

questions.question: In the compound H2N-CH2-CH2-CH2-COOH, the -NH2 group must be named as:
options: the substituent prefix '4-amino-', since -COOH outranks -NH2 as the principal characteristic group and is cited as the parent suffix instead
the parent suffix '-amine', giving a name like 'butanamine-4-oic acid'
nothing -- amines are never cited in the name when another functional group is present
the suffix '-amide', since nitrogen-containing groups are always named as amides
questions.explanation: Because a carboxylic acid has higher seniority than an amine in IUPAC nomenclature, -COOH becomes the parent suffix ('-oic acid') and -NH2 is demoted to the prefix 'amino-'.
questions.hint: Compare the seniority of -COOH and -NH2 in the IUPAC functional-group priority order.
distractor_logic: This incorrectly treats -NH2 as senior to -COOH and produces a name that doesn't follow correct IUPAC seniority or suffix rules at all.
Even when outranked, -NH2 must still be cited in the name, just as the prefix 'amino-' rather than as the parent suffix.
An amide specifically requires a C(=O)-NH2 linkage; a simple -NH2 group elsewhere on a chain is not an amide and is not named as one.

questions.question: The compound with a nitro group positioned para to the amino group on an aniline ring is correctly named:
options: 4-nitroaniline (p-nitroaniline)
2-nitroaniline (o-nitroaniline)
4-aminonitrobenzene
3-nitroaniline (m-nitroaniline)
questions.explanation: Aniline is retained as the parent name, and the nitro substituent's position (para, i.e., carbon 4) is cited as its locant.
questions.hint: Recall which ring position 'para' refers to relative to the amino group at position 1.
distractor_logic: This locant places the nitro group ortho to the amino group, not para, which does not match the described substitution pattern.
By nomenclature convention, aniline is used as the retained parent name when an amino group is present, rather than treating nitrobenzene as the parent with amino as a substituent.
This locant places the nitro group meta to the amino group, not para, which does not match the described substitution pattern.

questions.question: To convert bromoethane, CH3CH2Br, into propan-1-amine, CH3CH2CH2NH2 (one carbon more), the correct two-step sequence is:
options: excess NH3, with no further step needed
NaCN, followed by H2/Ni (or LiAlH4)
Br2/NaOH, followed by H2O
aqueous KOH, followed by H2/Ni
questions.explanation: Cyanide substitution first adds one carbon (giving propanenitrile), and reduction then converts the nitrile fully into the primary amine.
questions.hint: Which reagent both adds a carbon AND installs the nitrogen-containing group needed before reduction?
distractor_logic: Ammonolysis of bromoethane gives ethanamine (same carbon count as the halide, plus over-alkylation issues), not the one-carbon-longer propan-1-amine.
These are Hoffmann bromamide degradation reagents, which act on a primary AMIDE, not on an alkyl halide like bromoethane.
Aqueous KOH substitutes bromide with -OH, giving ethanol; this pathway has nothing to do with building the target amine.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly converts nitrobenzene into acetanilide?
options: reduce with Fe/HCl to give aniline, then acetylate with acetic anhydride
treat nitrobenzene directly with NaNO2/HCl at 0-5°C
reduce with Fe/HCl to give aniline, then brominate directly with bromine water
acetylate nitrobenzene directly with acetic anhydride, then reduce
questions.explanation: The nitro group is first reduced to the free amine, which is then acylated to give acetanilide.
questions.hint: The nitro group must first become an amine before any nitrogen-based reaction can be performed on it.
distractor_logic: Diazotization requires a primary AMINE as the starting material, not a nitro compound, so this step cannot be applied directly to nitrobenzene.
This gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline, not acetanilide; bromination is not the step needed here.
Acetic anhydride reacts with an amine's N-H; a nitro group has no such N-H, so this order would fail at the very first step.

questions.question: Reductive amination of butan-2-one, CH3COCH2CH3, with ammonia and H2/Ni gives:
options: butan-1-amine, CH3CH2CH2CH2NH2
N,N-dimethylbutan-2-amine
2-methylpropan-2-amine (tert-butylamine)
butan-2-amine, CH3CH(NH2)CH2CH3
questions.explanation: The carbonyl oxygen is replaced by -NH2 at the same carbon, so the branching pattern of the ketone carries over directly into the amine.
questions.hint: Reductive amination replaces the carbonyl oxygen with -NH2 at the same carbon.
distractor_logic: This straight-chain product places -NH2 at the wrong carbon; reductive amination installs -NH2 at the SAME carbon that bore the carbonyl group in butan-2-one, not at a terminal carbon.
Reductive amination with plain NH3 introduces only one substitution at nitrogen, giving a primary amine, not a tertiary amine with two methyl groups.
This carbon skeleton does not match butan-2-one's framework at all and cannot arise from its reductive amination.

questions.topic: Gabriel Synthesis and Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation
questions.question: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis applied to 1-bromobutane ultimately gives:
options: a mixture of butan-1-amine, N,N-dibutylamine, and tributylamine
butan-2-amine (sec-butylamine)
phthalic acid only, with no amine formed
butan-1-amine (n-butylamine), a pure primary amine
questions.explanation: Since only a single alkylation of the phthalimide anion occurs, followed by hydrolysis, the method delivers one clean primary amine product with no over-alkylation.
questions.hint: Does Gabriel synthesis allow more than one alkylation on the same nitrogen?
distractor_logic: Unlike direct ammonolysis, Gabriel synthesis allows only ONE alkylation on the phthalimide nitrogen, so no over-alkylated mixture forms.
SN2 substitution occurs at the same carbon that bore the leaving group in 1-bromobutane, preserving the straight-chain connectivity rather than rearranging to a secondary position.
Hydrolysis of the N-alkylphthalimide releases BOTH the phthalate byproduct AND the free primary amine; the amine is very much a product of this synthesis.

questions.topic: Gabriel Synthesis and Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation
questions.question: In Hoffmann bromamide degradation, migration of the R group from carbon to nitrogen during formation of the isocyanate intermediate proceeds with:
options: no stereochemical consequence at all, since R is never chiral in this reaction
retention of configuration at the migrating group
complete inversion of configuration at the migrating group
racemization of the migrating group
questions.explanation: This concerted migration keeps the spatial arrangement of the migrating group intact, unlike a stepwise ionic substitution.
questions.hint: Compare this concerted rearrangement mechanism with a typical SN2 substitution.
distractor_logic: R can in principle be a chiral center (in a suitably substituted amide), and the well-established retention outcome is a real, testable stereochemical feature of the reaction, not something to dismiss.
Unlike an SN2-type backside attack, this concerted migration proceeds WITH retention of configuration, not inversion.
Because the mechanism is concerted, with no free carbocation or radical intermediate forming at R, no racemization occurs.

questions.topic: Gabriel Synthesis and Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation
questions.question: Which pair of starting materials -- one used in Gabriel synthesis, one in Hoffmann bromamide degradation -- would BOTH ultimately give propan-1-amine, CH3CH2CH2NH2, as the final product?
options: 1-bromopropane (Gabriel) and propanamide, CH3CH2CONH2 (Hoffmann)
1-chloroethane (Gabriel) and pentanamide (Hoffmann)
1-bromobutane (Gabriel) and butanamide (Hoffmann)
1-bromopropane (for Gabriel synthesis) and butanamide, CH3CH2CH2CONH2 (for Hoffmann degradation)
questions.explanation: Gabriel synthesis on 1-bromopropane retains all 3 carbons to give propan-1-amine directly; Hoffmann degradation of the 4-carbon butanamide loses its carbonyl carbon to also give the same 3-carbon propan-1-amine.
questions.hint: Remember: Gabriel synthesis retains the halide's full carbon count; Hoffmann degradation loses exactly one carbon from the amide.
distractor_logic: Hoffmann degradation of the 3-carbon propanamide loses one carbon, giving ethanamine (2 carbons), NOT propan-1-amine.
Gabriel synthesis on chloroethane gives the 2-carbon ethanamine, and Hoffmann degradation of the 5-carbon pentanamide gives the 4-carbon butan-1-amine -- neither matches propan-1-amine.
Gabriel synthesis on 1-bromobutane retains all 4 carbons, giving butan-1-amine, not the 3-carbon propan-1-amine.
