options: amides and nitriles are always solids, and HNO2 only reacts with liquid or gaseous substrates
HNO2 physically cannot come into contact with amides or nitriles due to their larger molecular size
amides and nitriles do not contain a nitrogen atom at all, so this chemistry is simply impossible for them

it is specifically the free, basic, and nucleophilic nitrogen lone pair on an amine's nitrogen that attacks the electrophilic nitrosating species derived from HNO2; an amide's or nitrile's nitrogen lone pair is far less available (tied up in resonance or multiple bonding), so these functional groups do not undergo the same chemistry
questions.explanation: The reaction requires a genuinely nucleophilic nitrogen lone pair, which amines have but amides and nitriles largely lack.
questions.hint: Compare how available the nitrogen lone pair is in an amine versus in an amide (tied up with a carbonyl) or a nitrile (tied up in a triple bond).
distractor_logic: Physical state (solid/liquid/gas) is irrelevant to whether this class of reaction occurs; the determining factor is the electronic character/availability of the nitrogen lone pair.
Molecular size/steric bulk is not the reason; the key factor is the electronic availability of the nitrogen lone pair, which is fundamentally different in an amine versus an amide or nitrile.
Amides and nitriles certainly do contain nitrogen; the reason they don't undergo this chemistry is that their nitrogen lone pair is unavailable, not that nitrogen is absent.
mixed_topics: Carbylamine Reaction and Reaction with Nitrous Acid

questions.topic: Gabriel Synthesis and Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation
questions.question: A chemist wants pure bromobenzene starting from benzamide, C6H5CONH2. Which sequence works?
options: (i) direct treatment of benzamide with CuBr/HBr
(i) Gabriel synthesis directly on benzamide, (ii) Sandmeyer with CuBr/HBr
(i) Hoffmann bromamide degradation (Br2/NaOH) to give aniline, (ii) diazotization (NaNO2/HCl, 0-5°C), (iii) Sandmeyer reaction with CuBr/HBr
(i) reduction of benzamide with LiAlH4 to give benzylamine, (ii) diazotization, (iii) Sandmeyer with CuBr/HBr
questions.explanation: This sequence correctly converts the amide to the amine (losing the carbonyl carbon), then to the diazonium salt, then to the aryl bromide.
questions.hint: Compare what LiAlH4 reduction does to an amide's carbon count versus what Hoffmann degradation does.
distractor_logic: Sandmeyer-type reagents act specifically on a DIAZONIUM salt, not directly on an amide; benzamide must first be converted through aniline and then to the diazonium salt before this step becomes relevant.
Gabriel synthesis is not applicable here at all -- it requires an alkyl/aryl HALIDE and phthalimide as starting materials, not an amide as the substrate.

LiAlH4 reduction of an amide gives an amine with the SAME number of carbons (via full reduction of C=O to CH2), i.e., benzylamine C6H5CH2NH2 -- not aniline C6H5NH2 -- which would ultimately lead to a benzylic bromide, not bromobenzene itself.
mixed_topics: Gabriel Synthesis and Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation
Reactions of Diazonium Salts: Sandmeyer and Replacement Reactions

questions.question: Why must the diazonium salt used in an azo-coupling reaction be kept cold (0-5°C) right up until the coupling step, even though the coupling partner (e.g., phenol or N,N-dimethylaniline) is perfectly stable at room temperature?
options: both reagents are equally unstable above 5°C, so both must be kept cold
cold temperature is needed only to slow down the coupling reaction so it can be monitored visually

it is specifically the diazonium salt -- not the coupling partner -- that is thermally unstable and prone to decomposition (e.g., hydrolysis to a phenol) above about 5°C, so keeping the whole mixture cold preserves the diazonium electrophile until it can react with the coupling partner
cold temperature has nothing to do with the diazonium salt; it is required only because azo dyes decompose at room temperature
questions.explanation: Only the diazonium species is temperature-sensitive here; the coupling partner needs no special cold-temperature handling.
questions.hint: Which single species in this reaction is thermally unstable in the first place?
distractor_logic: Phenol and N,N-dimethylaniline are both perfectly stable, ordinary compounds at room temperature; only the diazonium salt itself carries this thermal instability.
The cold temperature isn't primarily about monitoring the reaction's progress; it's specifically about preventing decomposition of the unstable diazonium salt before coupling can occur.
The azo dye PRODUCT formed by the coupling reaction is generally quite stable at room temperature; it is the diazonium salt STARTING material, before coupling, that requires the cold conditions.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Amines: Hinsberg's Test
questions.question: A primary amine's own N-H bonds are not acidic enough to be removed by aqueous KOH, yet after that same amine is converted into its Hinsberg benzenesulfonamide (RNH-SO2C6H5), the one remaining N-H suddenly IS acidic enough to be deprotonated by KOH. What causes this dramatic change?
options: the amine's original N-H bonds were never real N-H bonds to begin with; only the sulfonamide N-H is a genuine N-H bond
KOH is simply a much stronger base than any acid the free amine was ever exposed to
sulfonylation converts the nitrogen atom into an entirely different, non-nitrogen atom

the adjacent, strongly electron-withdrawing sulfonyl (-SO2-) group stabilizes the negative charge left on nitrogen once that N-H is removed, unlike an ordinary amine's N-H, which is flanked only by an electron-donating alkyl or aryl group, not an electron-withdrawing one
questions.explanation: Conjugate-base stabilization by the neighboring -SO2- group is what raises the N-H's acidity so sharply in the sulfonamide.
questions.hint: Think about how an adjacent electron-withdrawing group stabilizes the anion left behind after a proton is removed.
distractor_logic: Both are perfectly ordinary N-H bonds chemically; what differs is the electronic environment surrounding each one, not whether they 'count' as real N-H bonds.

The amine's own N-H genuinely is not significantly acidic under any ordinary conditions; the change happens specifically because of the newly introduced adjacent sulfonyl group in the sulfonamide, not because of a change in the base's strength.
The nitrogen atom itself is unchanged by sulfonylation; only its immediate substituents and the resulting electronic environment around it change.
mixed_topics: Distinguishing Tests for Amines: Hinsberg's Test

questions.question: Direct nitration of acetanilide gives predominantly one isomer. What is the correct name of this major product, before any hydrolysis?
options: N-(2-nitrophenyl)acetamide (o-nitroacetanilide)
N-(4-nitrophenyl)acetamide (p-nitroacetanilide)
4-nitroaniline
N-(3-nitrophenyl)acetamide (m-nitroacetanilide)
questions.explanation: The acetamido group remains an ortho/para director, and steric/electronic factors favor the para product as major.
questions.hint: Remember that the nitrogen is still acylated at this stage -- name the compound accordingly.
distractor_logic: This names the minor ortho isomer, not the major PARA product that predominates in this nitration.

This name describes the FREE amine product obtained only after hydrolysis of the acetamido group; before hydrolysis, the nitrogen is still acylated, so the compound must be named as a substituted acetamide, not as a substituted aniline.
The acetamido group is an ortho/para director, not a meta director, so the meta isomer is not the major product.

questions.topic: Gabriel Synthesis and Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation
questions.question: Both Gabriel synthesis and Hoffmann bromamide degradation are valued specifically because they avoid a problem common to simpler amine-preparation routes. What is that shared problem, and how does each method sidestep it?
options: both avoid the problem of amines being colorless and therefore hard to detect, by producing colored amine products
both avoid the problem of aromatic amines being weaker bases than aliphatic ones, by exclusively producing aromatic amine products

both avoid the over-alkylation problem of direct ammonolysis/alkylation: Gabriel synthesis avoids it because only ONE alkylation step occurs on the phthalimide nitrogen (which has no further N-H once alkylated), and Hoffmann degradation avoids it entirely by not using an alkylating step at all, instead building the amine through a completely different rearrangement mechanism
both avoid the problem of low boiling points in small amines, by only ever producing large, high-molecular-weight amines
questions.explanation: Neither method relies on the repeated-alkylation chemistry that causes over-alkylation in simple ammonolysis.
questions.hint: Recall the specific complication that plagues simple ammonolysis and direct alkylation of amines with alkyl halides.
distractor_logic: Amines produced by these methods are ordinary colorless compounds, like any other simple amine; color/detectability is not a concern these methods are designed to address.
Neither method is restricted to aromatic amine products; in fact, Gabriel synthesis cannot make aromatic primary amines at all, and both are commonly used for ALIPHATIC amine targets.
Neither method is restricted to producing large amines; both can readily give quite small amine products, such as ethanamine.
mixed_topics: Gabriel Synthesis and Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation

questions.question: Two routes are proposed to introduce a bromine atom onto aniline's ring at the para position: Route A (acetylate, brominate, hydrolyze) and Route B (diazotize, then treat with CuBr/HBr). Which statement correctly evaluates the two?
options: both routes give the exact same final product, p-bromoaniline, just by different means

Route A retains the amino group in the final product (giving p-bromoaniline), whereas Route B, using CuBr/HBr on the diazonium salt, instead REMOVES the amino group entirely (replacing it with -Br), giving bromobenzene, not p-bromoaniline -- so the two routes give genuinely different final products despite both introducing a bromine atom
Route B always retains the amino group in the final product, just like Route A does
Route A is chemically impossible, since bromination of any acylated aniline derivative cannot occur
questions.explanation: The two routes diverge in whether the nitrogen substituent survives: Route A keeps it, Route B (via Sandmeyer) replaces it entirely.
questions.hint: Ask whether each route KEEPS the nitrogen substituent in the final product, or eventually REPLACES it.
distractor_logic: Route B (via the diazonium salt and CuBr/HBr) actually loses the amino group entirely in the process, giving bromobenzene (with no amino group left) rather than p-bromoaniline, so the two products are not the same.

Converting the amine to a diazonium salt and then treating it with a Sandmeyer-type reagent such as CuBr/HBr specifically REPLACES the nitrogen-containing group with the new substituent -Br; the amino group is not retained in this route, unlike in Route A.
Acetanilide's ring, though less activated than free aniline's, is still activated enough to undergo bromination readily, making Route A a perfectly standard, valid approach.
mixed_topics: Reactions of Diazonium Salts: Sandmeyer and Replacement Reactions
Acylation and Alkylation Reactions of Amines

questions.question: Among aniline, N-methylaniline, and N,N-dimethylaniline, which reacts with acetic anhydride to form an N-acyl product, and which does NOT react in this way at all?
options: all three react identically, since they all share the same aniline-based nitrogen
N-methylaniline does not react at all, since secondary amines cannot be acylated
aniline (primary, two N-H bonds) and N-methylaniline (secondary, one N-H bond) both react to form N-acyl products; N,N-dimethylaniline (tertiary, no N-H) does not undergo this acylation at all
N,N-dimethylaniline reacts fastest, since more alkyl substitution always increases reactivity toward acylating agents
questions.explanation: Acylation requires at least one available N-H, which only the primary and secondary amines in this set possess.
questions.hint: Count the available N-H bonds on each amine before deciding whether acylation can occur.
distractor_logic: The number of available N-H bonds (and resulting reactivity) varies significantly among the three, giving them clearly different behavior, not identical reactivity.
A secondary amine still has one N-H available and readily undergoes acylation, forming an N-substituted amide, just as a primary amine does.
More N-alkyl substitution actually REDUCES the number of available N-H bonds for acylation, and a fully substituted tertiary amine has none left to react in this way at all.
mixed_topics: Acylation and Alkylation Reactions of Amines

questions.question: A given primary amine can be made either by reductive amination of a ketone with ammonia, or by an entirely different route that happens to converge on the exact same molecule. Does the synthetic route used to prepare a given amine affect its final basicity?
options: this question cannot be answered, since basicity is not a well-defined property for synthesized amines

no -- once formed, a given amine's basicity depends only on its own structure (which groups are attached to nitrogen), not on which synthetic route was used to make it; two different routes converging on the identical molecule give identically basic products
yes -- amines made via an oxime-reduction route are inherently weaker bases due to residual oxygen contamination
yes -- the reductive amination route always gives a more basic product, since it uses ammonia directly
questions.explanation: Basicity is a property of the final structure, with no 'memory' of the synthetic path taken to reach it.
questions.hint: Ask whether basicity is a property of the final molecule, or of the path taken to make it.
distractor_logic: Basicity is a well-defined intrinsic molecular property, applicable equally to amines regardless of how they were synthesized.
A properly purified amine product contains no such residual oxygen; its basicity depends purely on its final structure, not on trace synthetic history.
Once the final amine is formed, its basicity is a property of its own structure alone, not a memory of which specific reagents were used during its synthesis.

questions.question: Aniline is only slightly soluble in water, YET it reacts vigorously and essentially completely with bromine water (which is mostly water) to precipitate 2,4,6-tribromoaniline. How can aniline react so readily with an aqueous reagent despite its limited water solubility?
options: bromine water is not really an aqueous reagent, so aniline's water solubility is irrelevant here
bromine water reacts with aniline entirely on the surface in a two-phase reaction, with no need for aniline to dissolve at all
aniline is actually highly water-soluble, so the premise of the question is incorrect

even a low equilibrium concentration of dissolved aniline is continuously and essentially irreversibly consumed by the very fast bromination reaction, which pulls more aniline into solution and allows the reaction to go to completion even though aniline itself isn't very water-soluble
questions.explanation: Le Chatelier-style replenishment: as dissolved aniline reacts and is consumed, more dissolves to take its place, until the reaction is complete.
questions.hint: Think about what continuously happens to the small amount of aniline that IS dissolved at any given moment.
distractor_logic: Bromine water is indeed a genuinely aqueous solution of Br2; the point of the question is specifically about how the reaction still proceeds efficiently despite aniline's limited solubility in that aqueous medium.

The accepted explanation is that the fast, essentially irreversible reaction continuously consumes the small amount of dissolved aniline, driving further dissolution and reaction until it goes to completion.

Aniline is indeed only moderately/slightly soluble in water at room temperature, being a fairly large, mostly hydrophobic molecule attached to just one polar -NH2 group; the premise is factually accurate.

questions.topic: Gabriel Synthesis and Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation
questions.question: Hoffmann bromamide degradation of 3-methylbutanamide, (CH3)2CHCH2CONH2, gives an amine correctly named:
options: 2-methylpropan-2-amine, (CH3)3CNH2
2-methylpropan-1-amine (isobutylamine), (CH3)2CHCH2NH2
butan-1-amine, CH3CH2CH2CH2NH2
3-methylbutan-1-amine, (CH3)2CHCH2CH2NH2
questions.explanation: The carbonyl carbon is lost, and the intact (CH3)2CHCH2- group migrates to nitrogen, giving this branched 4-carbon primary amine.
questions.hint: Identify which group is attached to the carbonyl carbon in the starting amide, and remember that this exact group migrates intact.
distractor_logic: This implies a skeletal rearrangement of the migrating group during the reaction, but Hoffmann rearrangement proceeds with retention of the EXISTING connectivity of the R group, not rearrangement to a different branching pattern.
This straight-chain product doesn't match the branched isobutyl (2-methylpropyl) group that was actually attached to the carbonyl carbon in the starting amide.
This product retains the same number of carbons as the starting amide (5), but Hoffmann degradation always loses the carbonyl carbon, so the product must have one carbon fewer, not the same.
mixed_topics: Gabriel Synthesis and Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation

questions.topic: Carbylamine Reaction and Reaction with Nitrous Acid
questions.question: Both the carbylamine test and acylation with acetyl chloride specifically require an available N-H bond to proceed cleanly. Yet a tertiary amine, having NO N-H at all, still shows SOME interaction with both acetyl chloride and (for an aromatic tertiary amine) HNO2. Reconcile this apparent inconsistency.
options: tertiary amines actually do have an N-H bond; the classification 'tertiary' is a misnomer in this context
both reactions proceed through the SAME mechanism and give the SAME type of stable product as they would with a primary amine
this is a genuine contradiction; a tertiary amine, having no N-H, should give absolutely no reaction with either reagent under any circumstances

a tertiary amine's lone pair can still act as a simple Lewis base/nucleophile toward acetyl chloride (forming a transient salt/adduct, not a permanent N-acyl product, since there's no N-H to lose), and a tertiary AROMATIC amine's activated ring (not its nitrogen) is what reacts with HNO2's electrophilic nitrosating species -- so some interaction occurs in both cases, but neither gives the stable, N-H-dependent product that a primary or secondary amine would
questions.explanation: The nitrogen lone pair can still act as a base even without an N-H to formally lose, and for the aromatic case the reactive site simply shifts to the ring itself.
questions.hint: Distinguish between what the nitrogen LONE PAIR can still do, and what specifically requires an N-H bond.
distractor_logic: A tertiary amine, by definition, has all three positions on nitrogen substituted by carbon groups and genuinely has no N-H bond at all -- this isn't a misnomer.

Neither reaction with a tertiary amine gives the same stable, N-H-substitution product that a primary amine would; the outcomes (a transient salt, or ring substitution) are fundamentally different in character.

A tertiary amine's lone pair remains chemically available as a Lewis base/nucleophile even without an N-H to lose, so some transient interaction -- or, for an aromatic tertiary amine's ring, an entirely different ring-based reaction -- can still occur.
mixed_topics: Carbylamine Reaction and Reaction with Nitrous Acid
Acylation and Alkylation Reactions of Amines

questions.topic: Reactions of Diazonium Salts: Sandmeyer and Replacement Reactions
questions.question: Phenol can be made either by hydrolyzing a diazonium salt (from aniline) or, in principle, by direct hydrolysis of chlorobenzene under forcing conditions. Why is the diazonium route generally the more practical, milder method?
options: the diazonium route is preferred only because chlorobenzene is more expensive than aniline, with no real chemical advantage
both methods actually require identical, equally harsh conditions, so there is no practical difference between them

hydrolysis of a diazonium salt to phenol proceeds readily on just warming in water, since the -N2+ leaving group departs very easily as N2 gas; direct hydrolysis of an aryl chloride, by contrast, requires very harsh conditions (high temperature and pressure, strong base) because a plain C-Cl bond on an unactivated benzene ring is far more resistant to nucleophilic substitution
direct hydrolysis of chlorobenzene is actually easier and preferred over the diazonium route in practice
questions.explanation: N2 is an exceptionally good leaving group, making diazonium hydrolysis far milder than displacing chloride from an ordinary, unactivated aryl chloride.
questions.hint: Compare how good a leaving group N2 is versus how good a leaving group Cl− is on an unactivated aromatic ring.
distractor_logic: Cost is not the primary reason; there is a genuine, substantial chemical/mechanistic advantage to the diazonium route in terms of how easily the leaving group departs.
The diazonium route proceeds under distinctly milder conditions (simple warming in water) than the forcing conditions needed to hydrolyze an unactivated aryl chloride directly.

This reverses the actual practical comparison -- direct hydrolysis of an aryl halide is notoriously difficult and requires forcing conditions, which is exactly why the milder diazonium route is generally preferred.
mixed_topics: Reactions of Diazonium Salts: Sandmeyer and Replacement Reactions

questions.question: Between aniline (C6H5NH2) and benzylamine (C6H5CH2NH2), which one's ring undergoes the dramatic activation described for aniline (e.g., reacting directly with bromine water to give a tribromo product without a catalyst), and why does the other NOT show this same activation?
options: benzylamine shows the dramatic activation instead, since it has an additional CH2 group that donates extra electron density to the ring
both show identical dramatic ring activation, since both contain the same -NH2 functional group somewhere in the molecule
neither shows dramatic ring activation, since -NH2 is never a strong activator in any aromatic amine

aniline shows this dramatic ring activation, because its nitrogen lone pair is directly conjugated with the ring (nitrogen attached straight to a ring carbon); benzylamine's nitrogen, separated from the ring by an intervening -CH2- group, cannot conjugate its lone pair into the ring at all, so its ring behaves essentially like ordinary, unactivated benzene toward electrophilic substitution
questions.explanation: Direct attachment to the ring is essential for resonance donation; an intervening sp3 carbon completely breaks that conjugation.
questions.hint: Check whether nitrogen is attached directly to the ring, or separated from it by an intervening carbon.
distractor_logic: A saturated -CH2- linker does not conjugate electron density into the ring the way a directly attached nitrogen lone pair does; benzylamine's ring is not dramatically activated by its remote amino group.

What matters is not merely the presence of -NH2 somewhere in the molecule, but whether its lone pair can directly conjugate into the ring, which requires nitrogen to be attached DIRECTLY to a ring carbon, as in aniline but not in benzylamine.
-NH2 directly attached to a ring (as in aniline) is in fact one of the strongest activating groups known for electrophilic aromatic substitution; this premise is incorrect.

questions.question: A chemist runs Hinsberg's test on the compound named 'N,N-diethylethanamine' (triethylamine, by its common name). Based on correctly parsing this IUPAC name, what result is expected?
options: no reaction with benzenesulfonyl chloride occurs (since this is triethylamine, a tertiary amine with no N-H); it separates out unchanged after KOH is added
a soluble sulfonamide salt forms in KOH, since this must be a primary amine based on the 'ethanamine' parent name
an insoluble sulfonamide precipitate forms, since 'N,N-diethyl-' indicates a secondary amine
the compound cannot react with benzenesulfonyl chloride at all because 'ethanamine' derivatives are chemically inert
questions.explanation: 'N,N-diethylethanamine' correctly parses as ethanamine's nitrogen bearing two additional ethyl groups -- i.e., three ethyl groups total on nitrogen -- making it the tertiary amine triethylamine.
questions.hint: Carefully count how many ethyl groups end up on nitrogen once you parse the full name, parent plus both N-substituents.
distractor_logic: While 'ethanamine' alone would indeed be a primary amine, the 'N,N-diethyl-' prefix adds two more substituents directly onto that same nitrogen, converting it into a tertiary amine overall, not a primary one.

'N,N-diethylethanamine' correctly parses as having TWO ethyl substituents on the nitrogen of the ethanamine parent, in addition to that parent's own attachment, giving a TERTIARY amine overall (triethylamine), not a secondary one.

Many ethanamine derivatives (primary or secondary ones) certainly DO react with benzenesulfonyl chloride; it is specifically the fact that this particular compound turns out to be tertiary, given its full substituent pattern, that explains the lack of reaction, not any general inertness of 'ethanamine derivatives'.
mixed_topics: Distinguishing Tests for Amines: Hinsberg's Test

questions.question: Butan-1-amine and diethyl ether, CH3CH2-O-CH2CH3, have very similar molecular masses. Which is expected to have the HIGHER boiling point, and why?
options: diethyl ether has the higher boiling point, since oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen and therefore always forms stronger intermolecular forces
diethyl ether has the higher boiling point because ethers are generally less volatile than amines of similar size
both compounds have essentially identical boiling points, since they have similar molecular masses

butan-1-amine has the higher boiling point, because its N-H bonds allow intermolecular hydrogen bonding, while diethyl ether's oxygen, lacking any O-H bond, cannot hydrogen-bond with other ether molecules at all
questions.explanation: Despite oxygen's higher electronegativity, diethyl ether has no O-H donor at all, so it cannot self-hydrogen-bond the way butan-1-amine's N-H can.
questions.hint: Check whether each molecule actually has a hydrogen atom attached to its electronegative atom, not just whether that atom is present.
distractor_logic: Electronegativity alone doesn't guarantee hydrogen bonding; diethyl ether has NO O-H bond to donate as a hydrogen bond, so despite oxygen's electronegativity, it cannot hydrogen-bond with itself the way butan-1-amine's N-H can.
This is not a general rule; in this specific and typical comparison, the amine's hydrogen-bonding capability (absent in the ether) gives it the higher, not lower, boiling point.

Despite similar molecular mass, their intermolecular forces differ substantially -- butan-1-amine can hydrogen-bond via N-H while diethyl ether cannot self-hydrogen-bond at all -- giving them clearly different boiling points.

questions.question: Would coupling proceed as readily between benzenediazonium chloride and p-nitroaniline as it does with plain aniline or phenol, under the usual mild coupling conditions?
options: no -- coupling would be much LESS effective (or fail to proceed under the usual mild conditions) with p-nitroaniline, because the strongly electron-withdrawing -NO2 group substantially deactivates the ring, counteracting -NH2's usual activating influence and leaving the ring far less nucleophilic toward the diazonium electrophile than plain aniline's ring would be
yes -- coupling would proceed even better with p-nitroaniline, since -NO2 makes the ring an even better electrophile for further reaction
whether coupling proceeds has nothing to do with the ring's substituents; it depends only on the diazonium salt's own structure
yes -- coupling would proceed identically well with p-nitroaniline, since -NH2 is present and is always a strong activator regardless of other substituents
questions.explanation: The competing -NO2 group's resonance withdrawal largely cancels -NH2's activation, leaving too little ring nucleophilicity for efficient coupling.
questions.hint: Weigh -NH2's activating resonance donation against -NO2's competing electron-withdrawing resonance effect on the same ring.
distractor_logic: -NO2 deactivates the ring toward attack BY an electrophile like the diazonium ion; it does not make the p-nitroaniline ring a better electrophile, and in any case this ring needs to act as the NUCLEOPHILE in a coupling reaction, not as an electrophile.

The second ring's (the coupling partner's) electronic character -- specifically how activated or deactivated it is -- is exactly what determines whether and how readily coupling proceeds; it is not solely dependent on the diazonium salt.
The presence of -NH2 alone doesn't guarantee strong activation if a powerful competing electron-withdrawing group like -NO2 is also present on the ring, substantially counteracting it.
